newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures finished the MATIF session marginally weaker, with the June 10-year future failing to push through resistance at 128.16 during Wednesday's early gains and later ebbing with German and U.S. debt futures.
Talk of a technical rebound, after five consecutive days of decline, came to little in rangebound, if see-saw, pit-trading.
The 10-year future could remain between 127.50 and 128.50 as markets wait for interest rate signals with the approach of the March 25 meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy council.
It settled at 127.90 on MATIF and dipped further on GLOBEX, down 0.26 at 127.58, as the Bund tumbled further on LIFFE.

U.S. treasuries were trading narrowly lower at the same time after a firmer start petered out in the wake of CPI data showing a 0.3 percent overall rise in February. It rose 0.2 percent with food and energy prices stripped out, in line with expectations.

After MATIF close, IMF chief economist Michael Mussa said the U.S. Fed "seems, with inflation at three percent or a little bit weaker, not to want to push to hard to drive it down", and added he saw possible room for easier monetary policy in Europe.
However, a German finance ministry official said at the same time, in Washington, a delay to European monetary union could not be ruled out, but that it was unlikely.

The official, speaking at an IMF-sponsored conference, also said Germany's debt would not make it down to the level of 60 percent of GDP which the Maastricht treaty calls on EU states to achieve or show they are heading towards.

"For me the most likely outcome is that we will start on time," Klaus Regling, Director General for European and International Financial Relations at the German ministry said on EMU. "But we can't exclude the other possibility."

Mussa, attending the IMF-sponsored conference on economic and monetary union, also said participants including academics and IMF and government officials agreed in the belief that EMU would probably be launched on time -- January 1, 1999.
